Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• 44-year-old physically active woman with 2-week history of right-dominant knee pain and clicking provoked by running (>20 min/≈3 mi) and leg-extension exercises; full ROM, no instability, locking, or current swelling; one transient swelling episode responsive to ice; single episode of right-toe tingling post-run.  
• Exam (video): no visible effusion, erythema, or warmth; able to fully flex/extend; pain localized “middle then right” of knee.  

Working diagnosis  
Patellofemoral pain syndrome (runner’s knee) – most consistent with over-use onset, activity-related pain, clicking, normal stability, and good response to rest/ice.

Supporting differentials  
• Patellar tendinopathy – activity-related anterior knee pain; consider if pain concentrates at inferior patella/tendon.  
• Degenerative/traumatic meniscal tear – prior hockey fall plus mechanical clicking; lower likelihood given absence of locking or persistent effusion.  
• Iliotibial band syndrome – lateral knee pain after mileage; less typical clicking.  

Management  
• Continue ice therapy after activity.  
• Temporarily reduce running mileage/intensity; cross-train with low-impact activities.  
• Prescribed stronger NSAID (specific agent not documented) to be used regularly with food and NOT concurrently with ibuprofen/naproxen; counsel on GI risk.  
• Referral to physiotherapist for comprehensive knee examination, gait assessment, and initiation of quadriceps/hip-strengthening program.  
• Arrange in-clinic review if physiotherapy wait is prolonged or if red-flag symptoms develop (persistent swelling/effusion, heat, redness, fever, inability to bear weight, locking).  
• Consider imaging (knee X-ray ± MRI) if no improvement or if exam suggests structural injury.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Patellofemoral pain syndrome – High likelihood; classic over-use anterior knee pain with running, clicking, normal stability.  
2. Patellar tendinopathy – Medium likelihood; activity-related pain with leg-extension, but clicking less typical.  
3. Meniscal tear – Medium likelihood; prior trauma and mechanical symptoms, but lacks locking/persistent swelling.
